name: Cutis tricolor
aliases: paired hyper- and hypopigmented macules with normal skin

reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Describes the coexistence of hyperpigmented and hypopigmented macules in close proximity against a background of normally pigmented skin
It is understood as an example of twin spotting (didymosis), in which two mosaic clones of opposite pigmentary tendency arise from a single post-zygotic event
The pigmentary lesions typically follow the lines of Blaschko or a segmental pattern reflecting their mosaic origin
It may occur in isolation or as part of a wider malformation syndrome with neurological and skeletal features
Reported associations include developmental delay, skeletal anomalies and, in some cases, features overlapping recognised overgrowth or dysmorphic syndromes
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by careful mapping of the paired pigmentary lesions
Management is generic: reassurance and cosmetic camouflage for isolated skin disease, with developmental and skeletal assessment where systemic features are present
reference.pathophysiology: Cutis tricolor is regarded as a pigmentary manifestation of twin spotting, in which a single post-zygotic somatic recombination event produces two genetically distinct daughter clones with opposing pigmentary behaviour, one hyperpigmented and one hypopigmented, adjacent to each other on a background of unaffected skin. Because the event occurs during embryonic development, the paired macules follow the lines of Blaschko or a segmental distribution. When the underlying mosaic clones also affect neuroectodermal or mesodermal tissue, the associated neurological and skeletal anomalies of the syndromic form arise, whereas involvement limited to melanocyte precursors produces isolated cutaneous disease.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated café-au-lait macules and naevus depigmentosus
Segmental pigmentary mosaicism (hypomelanosis of Ito, segmental hyperpigmentation)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed skin mapping of paired hyper- and hypopigmented lesions
Wood's lamp examination to accentuate hypopigmented macules
Skin biopsy where diagnosis is uncertain
Neurological and developmental assessment where systemic features are suspected
Skeletal imaging where deformity or asymmetry is present
MRI of the brain in patients with neurological symptoms
redFlags: Developmental regression or new neurological signs
Features suggesting a defined overgrowth or dysmorphic syndrome
reference.prognosis: Isolated cutis tricolor is benign with an excellent prognosis and is mainly of cosmetic significance, whereas the syndromic form carries a prognosis determined by the associated neurological and skeletal abnormalities.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnostic pairing of hyper- and hypopigmented lesions and treating each in isolation
Failing to assess for systemic involvement when pigmentary mosaicism is extensive
Confusing the hypopigmented component with vitiligo
Not using Wood's lamp, which can miss subtle hypopigmented macules
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Reassurance for isolated disease, which is benign and mainly of cosmetic significance
Cosmetic camouflage or laser treatment of the pigmentary macules where desired
Neurological and developmental assessment when systemic features suggest the syndromic form
Skeletal imaging and orthopaedic input where deformity or asymmetry is present
Brain MRI in patients with neurological symptoms
Multidisciplinary care through dermatology, neurology and clinical genetics, with genetic counselling for the mosaic twin-spotting mechanism
